title: Stop a bash script from running twice at the same time
summary: Uses a lock file so that only one copy of the script can work at a time. A second copy sees that the lock is taken and exits, and the lock is released automatically when the first copy ends.

aliases.text: only one instance of a script bash
prevent a bash script from running twice
stop second copy of script bash

steps.explain: Save the script. Create the file with nano and paste the whole text, including the first line that starts with #!. Press Ctrl+O then Enter to save, and Ctrl+X to exit.
steps.expect: An empty editor opens. After you save, the file exists in the current folder.

steps.explain: Check the script for syntax mistakes without running it.
steps.expect: No output means the syntax is correct.

steps.explain: Make the script executable so you can start it by its name.
steps.expect: No output. ls -l then shows x in the permissions.

steps.explain: Start one copy in the background with its own lock file, then start a second copy while the first is still busy. The second copy refuses to run and exits with code 1.
steps.cmd: LOCK_FILE=./demo.lock ./<FILE> & sleep 1; LOCK_FILE=./demo.lock ./<FILE>; echo exit code $?; wait
steps.expect: The second copy prints another copy is already running (lock file: ./demo.lock), exiting, then exit code 1. The first copy prints work finished.

steps.explain: After the first copy has finished, the lock is free again and a new run works.

warnings: Child programs inherit the lock. If the script starts a program in the background that keeps running after the script ends, the lock stays taken. Close the lock file in that child with 9>&-.
flock comes from util-linux and is available on Linux. On macOS, use a lock folder created with mkdir instead.
The default lock file is in /tmp, which all users can see. On a shared computer, set LOCK_FILE to a path only your user can write.

script.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# single-instance.sh - run a job only when no other copy of this script is running.
# Usage: ./single-instance.sh
# The lock file is $LOCK_FILE (default: /tmp/single-instance.lock).
# flock holds the lock while the file stays open, so the lock is released
# automatically when the script ends, even after a crash.

set -euo pipefail

LOCK_FILE=${LOCK_FILE:-/tmp/single-instance.lock}

# Open the lock file on file descriptor 9, then try to lock it without waiting (-n).
exec 9>"$LOCK_FILE"
if ! flock -n 9; then
    echo "another copy is already running (lock file: $LOCK_FILE), exiting" >&2
    exit 1
fi

echo "lock acquired (pid $$), doing the work for 3 seconds..."
sleep 3
echo "work finished"

prerequisites: A Linux terminal with bash 4 or newer
